articles.headline: HuggingFace Makes Knowledge Distillation Scalable and Affordable
articles.body: HuggingFace has released new tools and methods that dramatically reduce the cost and complexity of knowledge distillation — the process of compressing large AI models into smaller, faster versions while maintaining performance. Knowledge distillation works by training a smaller 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger 'teacher' model, enabling deployment on edge devices and production systems with lower computational overhead. Historically, this process required significant GPU resources and careful tuning, making it economically prohibitive for most teams. HuggingFace's approach includes optimized libraries, pre-configured training pipelines, and benchmarked recipes that reduce both the engineering effort and hardware costs required. The solution targets the gap between cutting-edge open-source models (which are powerful but expensive to run) and the need for fast, efficient inference in real-world applications. This matters because startups and enterprises building AI products often hit a wall: their models work in testing but become too slow or costly in production. By making distillation cheap and accessible, HuggingFace is enabling a new wave of AI applications where performance and cost-efficiency can coexist. The framework supports major model families including Llama, Mistral, and other open-source architectures, making it immediately applicable to existing projects.
examples: Compress a 70B parameter model into a 7B version that runs 10x faster with minimal accuracy loss.
Distill proprietary fine-tuned models into production-ready versions that fit on consumer hardware.

articles.headline: TutorMoments: The AI tutor that knows when NOT to help you
articles.body: TutorMoments is tackling one of the biggest problems in AI-powered education: knowing when to give hints versus full answers. The platform uses adaptive learning logic to decide in real-time whether a student needs scaffolding, a nudge, or should be left to figure it out themselves. This matters because research shows that immediate answers actually hurt learning—students need productive struggle to build real understanding. TutorMoments trains on interaction patterns to recognize when a student is genuinely stuck versus when they're just looking for the easy way out. The system can adjust its intervention level dynamically, sometimes asking clarifying questions instead of solving the problem, sometimes breaking it into smaller steps, and sometimes stepping away entirely. For educators and tutoring platforms, this solves the 'lazy student problem'—the tool prevents users from gaming the system while maintaining engagement. Real-world impact: tutoring companies can now offer personalized help at scale without the pedagogical cost of AI that's too generous with answers. The catch is that this requires careful calibration per subject and age group, so implementation isn't one-size-fits-all.

articles.hook: Meta just rewrote how ads load at lightning speed.
articles.headline: Meta Ditches Linux Kernel Limits With Custom Open-Source Scheduler
articles.body: Meta faced a critical problem: upgrading Linux kernels across its massive ad-serving infrastructure risked adding milliseconds of latency, which directly tanks ad performance and revenue at their scale. Rather than accept the degradation, Meta's engineering team built a custom scheduling policy using sched_ext — an upstream, BPF-based extensible scheduling framework available in modern Linux kernels. This approach lets them optimize scheduling decisions specifically for ad delivery workloads without waiting for generic kernel improvements. The solution is open-source, meaning other companies running high-performance services can adopt and adapt it. By controlling how CPU resources are allocated to ad-serving processes at the kernel level, Meta can maintain sub-millisecond latency guarantees even as systems scale. This is a fundamental shift: instead of being constrained by generic OS scheduling, companies can now write custom scheduling policies tailored to their exact workload. The framework uses eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter), which lets Meta push custom logic into the kernel safely without forking Linux or maintaining proprietary patches. For ad platforms, CDNs, and trading systems where microseconds matter, this represents a new lever for performance optimization that was previously unavailable.
examples: Write custom CPU scheduling rules in eBPF that optimize specifically for ad-serving latency patterns.
Deploy kernel-level scheduling changes without upgrading the entire Linux distribution across thousands of servers.
Monitor and adjust how processes compete for CPU resources in real-time based on workload telemetry.
articles.build: Infrastructure teams at agencies and ad networks can license or build custom schedulers on top of sched_ext to reduce latency in their own ad-serving stacks — reducing auction delays and improving win rates. articles.headline: Google's Free AI Agents Course Hits 353K Learners in Kaggle Intensive
articles.body: Google and Kaggle launched an AI Agents Intensive course at zero cost, attracting 353,000 learners eager to build and deploy AI agents—the frontier of autonomous AI systems. The course teaches participants how to architect, train, and deploy intelligent agents capable of taking actions, making decisions, and solving complex problems without constant human intervention. This represents a significant democratization moment: previously, building production-grade AI agents required expensive infrastructure, specialized expertise, and proprietary frameworks. Now learners can access Google's own tools and methodologies directly through Kaggle's platform. The course covers practical agent architectures, integration with Google's AI models, deployment strategies, and real-world use cases across industries from customer service automation to research assistance. By making this free and at scale, Google is seeding a generation of creators who'll build the next wave of AI applications—and many will become customers for Google Cloud's paid infrastructure as their projects grow. The timing is strategic: AI agents are moving from research labs into production, and first-mover advantage goes to developers with practical experience.

articles.hook: Google just made building AI agents way less painful.
articles.headline: Google Launches Gemini Managed Agents with 3.6 Flash, Hooks, and Production-Ready Features
articles.body: Google has announced significant new capabilities for Managed Agents in the Gemini API, enabling developers to build reliable, production-ready AI agents more efficiently. The update includes support for Gemini 3.6 Flash, Google's latest and fastest model, which provides improved performance and reduced latency for agent workflows. The release introduces 'hooks'—developer tools that allow deeper customization and control over agent behavior at critical execution points, giving builders more flexibility in how agents handle tasks, make decisions, and interact with external systems. These hooks enable developers to inject custom logic into the agent pipeline without rewriting core functionality, reducing development time and increasing reliability. The update addresses a key pain point in agent development: production systems require predictability, error handling, and the ability to intervene in agent decision-making without rebuilding entire systems. Managed Agents abstracts away infrastructure complexity—developers no longer need to handle model deployment, scaling, or monitoring themselves. With 3.6 Flash's speed improvements and the new hooks architecture, developers can now build agents that are not only intelligent but also maintainable and debuggable at scale. This positions Gemini API as a more complete solution for teams building autonomous systems, competing directly with other platforms offering agent frameworks and managed services.
examples: Deploy a customer service agent that automatically handles tickets, escalates complex issues to humans via custom hooks.
Build a data analysis agent that queries databases, validates results, and flags anomalies before returning insights.
Create a task automation agent that chains multiple APIs together while logging every decision point for audit trails.
